author: TGEU
title: Trans Murder Monitoring 2026 shows that every 32 hours, a trans person was murdered
content:
TGEU’s Trans Murder Monitoring (TMM) has recorded 273 trans and gender diverse people murdered worldwide over the past year, on average, one murder reported every 32 hours. Murders were reported across 35 countries, the second-highest number since the monitoring began, and for the first time in Romania and Cameroon. In total, TMM has now recorded over 5,500 murders globally since data collection began in 2009. 




TGEU – Trans Europe and Central Asia publishes the annual update of its global Trans Murder Monitoring project in the lead-up to Trans Awareness Week, ending with the Trans Day of Remembrance (TDoR) on 20 November. 




The TMM project counts only reported murders, and monitoring work is getting harder. The total number of reported murders is under 300 for only the second time in a decade, but the violence has not eased. Shrinking civic space, media and state-backed hostility towards trans people, and cuts to funding make it less likely that a murder is reported and recorded. 




Read in:

 

Portuguese

 ┃

Spanish

┃ 

Russian




Key findings







273 trans and gender diverse people were reported murdered

 between 1 October 2025 and 30 September 2026 – 

one murder every 32 hours

.




35 different countries

 reported a murder – 

the second highest ever

. Only in 2024 was the number of reporting countries higher (38).




One in three victims were sex workers (

32%

), who remain the most targeted group

 of all known occupations. 




Echoing the patterns of previous years, 

almost all reported murders (95%) were feminicides

 (victims were trans women or transfeminine people), and 

three-quarters (75%) of victims were Black or Brown trans people.




The age profile of murder victims appears to be shifting 

slightly older

. More than one third (35%) were aged 

31-40

 in 2026, while one in five (21%) victims were aged 

19-25

 – consistently the largest age group in the first decade of TMM. One in twenty (5%) victims in the past year were 

minors under the age of 18

.




Seven out of ten (

69%)

 

murders occurred in Latin America and the Caribbean

. Brazil leads the list once again, accounting for one in three (32%) of the global total. Numbers continued to fall in 

Mexico

, with the lowest reported murders (29) since 2011. However, 2026 saw the highest-ever total in 

Argentina

 (16) and the second-highest total in 

Ecuador

 (16) since TMM began.




The number of reported murders in 

Asia

 (32) fell after last year’s all-time high (51). This year’s total is 

likely an undercount

 – some monitoring partners in Asia reported no capacity to provide data this year, citing lack of resources and even electricity.




13 murders were reported in Europe, 

the highest total since 2023

 – as many as 2024 and 2025 combined. The 

majority of victims were international migrants

.




One in ten murders were recorded in the 

United States

 (29), a similar level to 2025 (31).




Two in five (40%) reported murders were 

shootings

, while a quarter (24%) were 

stabbings

. Three in ten (30%) of murders occurred on the 

street

, and one quarter (25%) occurred in the victim’s own 

home

.




Of known perpetrators, one in four (25%) were a current or former partner, lover or spouse. Other commonly reported perpetrators were organised hate groups/gangs (15%), strangers (14%), police/military/army (12%) and sex work clients (8%).




A 

perpetrator was

 

arrested

 in only one in five murders (21%) where local authorities documented a response.










Intersectional violence




Year after year, the same demographic of trans people are murdered. Almost all reported victims (95%) were trans women or transfeminine people. Sex workers, who make up one in three victims, remain the most targeted group of all known occupations, and three in four victims were Black or Brown trans people.




This is what intersecting oppression looks like in practice. Misogyny, transphobia, racism, xenophobia and whorephobia compound one another, and those at their crossroads are the ones most at risk. 




“As a Black trans woman and a refugee, I live with the constant fear of losing my life. While others go about their daily lives with a sense of safety, Black trans women must remain vigilant, always watching our backs. Our safety is never guaranteed.




These murders are not just numbers in a report; they are our friends, colleagues, siblings, parents, and members of our communities. As these killings increase year after year, we demand more than sympathy: we demand justice, proper investigations, and accountability for every life taken. Black trans women deserve the right to live safely, freely, and with dignity.”




– Purity Tumukwasibwe, TGEU Board member  







Most reported murders: Latin America and the Caribbean




Behind the global total, the violence is not evenly spread. Seven in ten of this year’s reported murders took place in Latin America and the Caribbean, and Brazil again accounts for one in three murders worldwide.




The concentration reflects the scale of violence, and it also reflects documentation. Latin America has a long-established movement of trans and feminist organisations that monitor and report feminicides. As a result, more murders reach the record than in regions where that infrastructure is thin. The figures are also raw counts, not adjusted for population size, so they show where murders are reported, not where a trans person is at greatest risk. 




Within the region, the picture moves in different directions. Some countries appear to be on a downward trajectory (e.g. Mexico), while others have reached the highest annual total since our monitoring began (e.g. Argentina). A lower national figure should not be read as a safer country without looking closely at each context, as one of our monitoring partners points out:




‘We must not show any signs of celebration [over the decline in recorded murders]; rather, we must scrutinise current trends, including those in each individual country.’

 




– Rocío Suárez, Centro de Apoyo a las Identidades Trans A.C., Mexico







Our region: Europe and Central Asia




In Europe, 13 murders were reported this year. That is as many as in 2024 and 2025 combined. Most victims were international migrants; almost all were trans women or transfeminine people, and a third were sex workers. The pattern is clear: those at the intersection of multiple forms of marginalisation are the most at risk. 




Many people come to Europe in search of a life in which they can be themselves and be safe. For the migrants among these victims, that search ended in murder. The pattern points to the combined effect of xenophobia, racism and transphobia, which leaves trans migrants without protection and among the most exposed to harm. This comes amid a growing far-right and anti-gender backlash across Europe, translating into increasingly hostile rhetoric, restrictive legislation and political attacks on the rights of migrants and trans people.




In Central Asia, no murders were reported to us this year. This should not be read as an absence of violence. It more likely reflects a lack of safety for trans people in the region, forced to remain as invisible as possible, while their relatives may not disclose their trans identity after death. With activists facing overwhelming challenges and limited resources for monitoring, murders often go uncounted. One of the victims killed in Europe this year was a migrant from Central Asia, which echoes a wider story of trans people leaving the region to build a life where they can live more openly.




“Laws that target the rights of migrants and asylum seekers—especially racialised people from the Global South—and criminalise sex work are State tools that enable the murder of trans migrant women and trans sex workers. We must keep fighting back against these laws and building caring, strong and resistant communities. Fascism and fortresses will fall only through our collective struggles and through allyships with those at the margins and with colonised peoples.”




–  Tayri Fadil, TGEU Board member 







Who is behind trans murders?




Where the perpetrator was known, one in five murders (19%) was committed by a partner, lover or spouse.  Almost a quarter of this year’s murders (25%) took place in the victim’s own home. It is a pattern that echoes previous years: in a society hostile to trans people, even one’s own home is not a safe place.




Organised hate groups and gangs (15%) and strangers (14%) were also commonly reported. Together, these patterns point to violence that reaches trans people everywhere: in their relationships, in their communities, and on the street.




In 12% of cases where the perpetrator was known, the person responsible was a member of the police, military, or army: 13 murders, up from five last year. Nine trans people were murdered or died in suspicious circumstances in prisons or police stations, compared with four last year. These are state institutions, and deaths inside them are violence committed or allowed by the state.




These figures raise hard questions about who is protected, and who is not. Trans people are exposed to hostility, profiling and abuse by state actors, and those with a duty to uphold the law are among those responsible for taking trans lives. When transphobia and transmisogyny shape how these institutions operate, trans people are left more exposed.




When local authorities responded, a perpetrator was arrested in only one in five cases (21%). Judicial processes take time, and some cases move slowly through the system. However, many murders of trans people are not investigated at all; others are investigated without urgency, or are not recorded for what they are. Bias in how murders are investigated and ruled on, including the dismissal of anti-trans motives, means those responsible are less likely to be held to account. For families and communities, the absence of justice can be another loss.




“Every year we witness the predictable result of the systemic hate and repression of trans lives. While remembering our lives, I want to also name who kills us: family members, partners, clients, police, and the institutions that let them. It’s time they answer for it.”




– Isa Nico Borrelli, TGEU Board Chair







Demographic trends




The pattern of who is most at risk has not changed. One in three victims were sex workers, the most targeted group of all known occupations. Almost all (95%) were trans women or transfeminine people, and 76% were Black or Brown trans people.




Recorded victims appear to be getting slightly older, with one in three aged 31 to 40, while one in twenty were minors. Furthermore, reported murders in Asia fell from last year’s all-time high of 51 to 32. This is likely an undercount: some monitoring partners in the region lacked the capacity to provide data this year, citing a lack of electricity and funding.







Recommendations 




TGEU calls on  governments and institutions to:







Repeal laws and policies that criminalise or restrict trans identities, legal gender recognition, trans specific healthcare, and the public expression of trans and gender diverse identities.




End the criminalisation of sex work in full and guarantee labour rights and protections for trans and gender-diverse sex workers.




Harmonise and adopt hate crime and anti-discrimination laws that explicitly protect trans people in employment, education, and other areas, and work towards a shared understanding of what counts as illegal hate speech.




Ensure prison placement decisions are based on self-determination, irrespective of legal gender recognition status, and include the wishes and welfare of the trans person concerned.




Back trans human rights defenders and civil society organisations by relieving financial pressures, safeguarding their security, and allowing them to keep organising and advocating for their rights without fear.




Train professionals to respond appropriately to anti-trans violence, including police forces, with particular attention to those facing intersecting forms of discrimination, including Black trans women and sex workers.




For EU countries, ensure fully trans-inclusive and timely transposition and implementation of the EU Directive on combating violence against women and domestic violence.

Note on the term feminicide




TMM uses 

feminicide

 rather than 

femicide

 as it better reflects the structural and political causes of violence against women and girls. Coined by Marcela Lagarde in Latin America, the term highlights state responsibility and the systemic failures of prevention, protection, and accountability that enable such murders.




More information







Look at the 

global map

 of all reported murders (Jan 2008 – Sep 2026; EN, ES, RU, PT)

case library

 (Jan 2008 – Sep 2026; EN, ES, RU, PT)

visualisations

 of all-time demographic data (Jan 2008 – Sep 2026; EN, ES, RU, PT)

demographics tables

 (Oct 2025 – Sep 2026; EN, ES)

namelist

 for TDoR vigils (Oct 2025 – Sep 2026; EN, ES;

,

)

We work across Europe and Central Asia to advance trans rights, build strong communities, and drive change through research, advocacy, and community-building.




Your donation helps us continue this vital work — defending trans lives, amplifying trans voices, and advocating for justice every day.

author: TGEU
title: A Monitorização de Assassinato Trans de 2026 mostra que a cada 32 horas, uma pessoa trans foi morta.
content:
A Monitorização de Assassinato Trans [Trans Murder Monitoring] (TMM) da TGEU registou 273 pessoas trans e de género diverso assassinadas mundialmente ao longo do ano passado, em média, um homicídio registado a cada 32 horas. Assassinatos foram registados em 35 países, o segundo número mais elevado desde que a monitorização começou, e pela primeira vez na Roménia e no Camarões. No total, a TMM registou até à data mais de 5,500 assassinatos globalmente desde que a recolha de dados começou em 2009.




A TGEU – Trans Europe and Central Asia publica a actualização anual do seu projecto global Monitorização de Assassinato Trans no âmbito da Semana de Consciencialização Trans, que termina com o Dia da Memória Trans (TDoR) a 20 de Novembro.




O projecto da TMM conta apenas com números registados, e o trabalho de monitorização está a tornar-se mais difícil. O número total de assassinatos registados é inferior a 300 apenas pela segunda vez numa década, mas a violência não terminou. O espaço cívico em declínio, a hostilidade contra pessoas trans incentivada pela media e pelo estado, e cortes a financiamento tornam menos provável que um assassinato seja relatado e registado.




Principais Conclusões







273 pessoas trans e de género diverso foram registadas como assassinadas

 entre 1 de Outubro de 2025 e 30 de Setembro de 2026 – um assassinato a cada 32 horas.




35 países diferentes

 registaram um assassinato – 

o segundo maior número de sempre

. Apenas em 2024 os números de países com dados foram mais altos (38).




Uma em três vítimas eram trabalhadoris do sexo (32%), que continuam a ser o grupo mais atingido

 de todas as ocupações.




Ecoando os padrões de anos anteriores, 

quase todos os assassinatos registados (95%) foram feminicídios

 (vítimas foram mulheres trans ou pessoas transfemininas), e 

três quartos (75%) das vítimas eram pessoas Negras ou Marrom trans

.




O perfil etário das vítimas de assassinato parece estar a mudar para uma 

idade ligeiramente  mais avançada

. Mais de um terço (35%) tinham idades compreendidas entre os 

31-40

 anos em 2026, enquanto uma em cinco (21%) das vítimas tinham idades entre os 

19-25

 – o que era, consistentemente o maior grupo etário na primeira década da TMM. Uma em vinte (5%) das vítimas do ano anterior foram 

menores de 18 anos de idade

.




Sete em cada dez (69%) dos assassinatos ocorreram na América Latina e nas Caraíbas

. O Brasil lidera na lista mais uma vez, representando um em três (32%) do total mundial. Números continuam a cair no 

México

, com o número mais baixo de assassinatos registados (29) desde 2011.




No entanto, 2026 viu o mais alto total de sempre na 

Argentina

 (16) e o segundo maior no 

Equador

 (16) desde que o TMM começou.




O número de assassinatos registados na 

Ásia

 (32) caiu desde o mais alto de sempre do ano passado (51). O total deste ano é 

muito provavelmente uma subcontagem

 – alguns parceiros na Ásia relataram não terem capacidade para fornecer dados este ano, citando falta de recursos e até mesmo de eletricidade.




13 assassinatos foram registados na Europa, 

o total mais elevado desde 2023

 – tantos como 2024 e 2025 combinados. A 

maioria das vítimas eram migrantes internacionais

.




Um em dez assassinatos foram registados nos 

Estados Unidos

 (29), um valor semelhante a 2025 (31).




Dois em cinco (40%) dos assassinatos registados foram 

a tiro

, enquanto que um quarto (24%) foram 

por esfaqueamento

. Três em dez (30%) dos assassinatos ocorreram na 

rua

, e um quarto (25%) ocorreram 

na casa

 da própria vítima.




Dos autores dos crimes de que se tem conhecimento, um em cada quatro (25%) era um ex ou actual parceiro, namorado ou marido. Outros autores comuns dos crimes registados eram grupos/gangues organizados de ódio (15%), estranhos (14%), polícia/militares/exército (12%) e clientes de trabalhadoras do sexo (8%).




Apenas um  agressor foi preso

 em cinco assassinatos (21%) onde autoridades locais documentaram uma resposta.










Violência Interseccional




Ano após ano, o mesmo perfil demográfico de pessoas trans são assassinadas. Quase todas as vítimas registadas (95%) foram mulheres trans e pessoas transfemininas. Trabalhadoras do sexo, que fazem uma em cada três vítimas, permanecem o grupo mais atingido de todas as ocupações, e três em quatro vítimas eram pessoas Negras ou Marrom de experiência trans.




Isto é como a opressão de intersecção se parece na prática. Misoginia, transfobia, racismo, xenófobia e putofobia se reforçam mutuamente, e aquelis que se encontram nesta encruzilhada, são es que mais estão em risco.




“C

omo mulher Negra trans e como refugiada, eu vivo no medo constante de perder a minha vida. Enquanto outres seguem o seu dia-a-dia com um sentido de segurança, mulheres Negras trans necessitam manter-se vigilantes, sempre a proteger a si mesmas. A nossa segurança nunca é garantida. 




Estes assassinatos não são só números num relatório; são nosses amigues, colegas, irmãos, pais, e membros das nossas comunidades. À medida que estes assassinatos sobem de número ano após ano, exigimos mais do que solidariedade: exigimos justiça, investigações adequadas, e responsabilização por cada vida ceifada. Mulheres Negras trans merecem o direito de viver de forma segura, livre e com dignidade.

”




– Purity Tumukwasibwe, membro da direção da TGEU







Maior número de assassinatos: América Latina e Caraíbas




Subjacente ao total global, a violência não está igualmente repartida. Sete em cada dez dos assassinatos registados neste ano tiveram lugar na América Latina e no Caribe, e mais uma vez o Brasil representa um em cada três assassinatos a nível mundial.




A concentração reflecte a escala da violência, e também reflecte a sua documentação. A América Latina possui um movimento há muito estabelecido de organizações trans e feministas que monitorizam e relatam feminicídios. Como resultado, mais assassinatos chegam aos registos do que em regiões onde essa infraestrutura é fraca. Estes números são também contagens em bruto, não ajustados à dimensão populacional, por isso eles mostram onde os assassinatos são registados, não onde uma pessoa trans está em maior risco.




Dentro da região, a imagem tende em direcções diferentes. Alguns países parecem estar numa trajectória descendente (e.g. México), enquanto outros atingiram ao mais alto total anual desde que a nossa monitorização começou (e.g. Argentina). Um balanço nacional mais baixo não deve ser lido como um país mais seguro sem observar cuidadosamente cada contexto, como uma das nossas parceiras de monitorização aponta:




‘

Não devemos mostrar qualquer sinal de celebração (em relação à descida de assassinatos registados); em vez disso, devemos escrutinizar as tendências actuais, incluindo as que existem em cada país individual.

‘




– Rocío Suárez, Centro de Apoyo a las Identidades Trans A.C., México







A nossa região: Europa e Ásia Central




Na Europa, 13 homicídios foram registados este ano. Esse número é equivalente ao de 2024 e 2025 combinados. A maior parte das vítimas eram migrantes internacionais; quase todas eram mulheres trans ou pessoas trans femininas, e um terço eram trabalhadoras do sexo. Este padrão é claro: aqueles que estão na interseccção de múltiplas formas de marginalização estão em maior risco.




Muitas pessoas vêm para a Europa na busca duma vida na qual elas podem ser elas mesmas e estar seguras. Para as pessoas migrantes entre estas vítimas, essa busca terminou em homicídio.  O padrão aponta para o  efeito combinado da xenofobia, racismo e transfobia, o que deixa migrantes trans sem protecção e entre es mais expostos a danos. Isto se sucede no meio de retaliação por parte de grupos de extrema-direita e anti-género sobre a Europa, traduzindo-se em crescente retórica hostil, legislação restritiva, e ataques políticos contra os direitos de migrantes e pessoas trans.




Na Ásia Central, nenhum assassinato nos foi reportado este ano. Isto não deve ser lido como uma ausência de violência. Muito provavelmente reflecte uma falta de segurança para pessoas trans na região, forçada a manter-se invisível o mais possível, enquanto os seus parentes podem não revelar a sua identidade trans depois da morte. Com activistas enfrentando desafios tremendos e recursos limitados para monitorização, assassinatos normalmente não são contabilizados.  Uma das vítimas mortas na Europa este ano era uma migrante da Ásia Central, o que ecoa uma estória mais abrangente de pessoas trans deixando a região para construir uma vida onde possam viver mais abertamente.




“Leis que atingem os direitos de migrantes e reivindicantes de asilo- especialmente pessoas racializadas do Sul Global- e que criminalizam o trabalho do sexo, são ferramentas do Estado que permitem o assassinato de mulheres trans migrantes e trabalhadoras trans do sexo. Devemos continuar a opôr-nos contra estas leis e continuar a construir comunidades carinhosas, fortes e resistentes. O Fascismo e as suas fortalezas caírão somente através dos nossas esforços colecivos e através de alianças com aquelis que estão nas margens e com povos colonizados.”




–  Tayri Fadil, Membro da Direcção da TGEU







Quem está por detrás dos assassinatos trans?




Nos casos em que o autor do crime era conhecido, um em cada cinco assassinatos (19%) foram cometidos por um parceiro, namorado ou marido. Quase um quarto dos assassinatos este ano (25%) ocorreram  na casa da própria vítima. É um padrão que ecoa o de anos passados: numa sociedade hostil a pessoas trans, mesmo a casa da própria pessoa não é um sítio seguro.




Grupos de ódio organizados e gangues (15%) e estranhos (14%) foram também comumente relatados. Juntos, estes padrões apontam para violência que atinge pessoas trans em todo o lado: nas suas relações, nas suas comunidades e na rua.




Em 12% dos casos onde o autor do crime era conhecido, a pessoa responsável era membro da polícia, militar ou do exército: 13 assassinatos, aumentando de cinco no ano passado. Nove pessoas trans foram mortas ou morreram em circunstâncias suspeitas em prisões ou esquadras de polícia, em comparação com quatro ano passado. Estas são instituições do estado, e mortes que se sucedem nelas são violência cometida ou permitida pelo estado.




Estes números levantam questões difíceis sobre quem é protegido, e quem não é. Pessoas trans são expostas a hostilidade, perfilamento e abuso por intervenientes estatais, e aqueles com o dever de manter a lei são responsáveis por ceifar vidas. Quando a transfobia e a transmisoginia moldam como estas instituições operam, pessoas trans ficam mais expostas.




Quando autoridades locais reagiram, um agressor foi preso apenas em um de cinco casos (21%). Processos judiciais levam tempo, e em alguns casos, avançam lentamente pelo sistema. No entanto, muitos assassinatos de pessoas trans não são investigados de todo; outros são investigados sem urgência, ou não são registados pelo que são. Preconceito em como homicídios são investigados e pautados, incluíndo o dispensar de motivos anti-trans, significa que os responsáveis terão menos probabilidade de serem chamados a prestar contas. Para famílias e comunidades, a ausência de justiça pode ser outra perda.




“Todos os anos, testemunhamos o resultado previsível do ódio sistémico e da repressão de vidas trans. Ao mesmo tempo que lembramos as nossas vítimas, quero também nomear quem nos mata: membros da família, parceires, clientes, polícia, e as instituições que lhes permitem. Está na altura de que respondam por isso.”




– Isa Nico Borrelli, Membro da Direcção da TGEU







Tendências demográficas




O padrão de quem mais está em risco não mudou. Uma em três vítimas eram trabalhadoras do sexo, o grupo mais atingido de todas as ocupações. Quase todas (95%) foram mulheres trans ou pessoas transfemininas, e 76% eram pessoas Negras ou Marrom de experiência trans.




As vítimas registadas se afiguram ser ligeiramente mais velhas, sendo uma em três entre os 31 e 40 anos de idade, enquanto que uma em vinte eram menores. Para além disso, os números registados na Ásia caíram desde o maior recorde de sempre no ano passado de 52 para 32. Isto é muito provavelmente uma subcontagem: alguns parceiros de monitorização na região não tinham capacidade de fornecer dados este ano, citando a falta de eletricidade e financiamento.







Recomendações




A TGEU convoca governos e instituições a:







Revogar leis e políticas que criminalizem ou restrinjam identidades trans, reconhecimento legal de género, cuidados médicos específicos para pessoas trans, e a expressão pública de identidades trans e de género diverso.




Terminar a criminalização do trabalho do sexo em pleno e garantir direitos laborais e protecções para trabalhadoris do sexo de experiência trans e de género diverso.




Harmonizar e adoptar leis anti-crime e anti-discriminação que explicitamente protejam pessoas trans na empregabilidade, educação, e outras áreas, e trabalhar rumo a um entendimento comum sobre o que conta como discurso de ódio ilegal.




Assegurar que decisões de encarceramento sejam baseadas na auto-determinação, independentemente do estatuto de reconhecimento do género legal, e incluir os desejos e bem-estar das pessoas trans em questão.




Apoiar defensoras de direitos humanos trans e organizações de serviço social aliviando pressões financeiras, salvaguardando a sua segurança, e permitindo-lhes continuar a organizar-se para defender os seus direitos sem medo.




Treinar profissionais para que respondam apropriadamente a violência anti-trans, incluindo as forças policiais, com atenção particular àquelas que enfrentam formas de intersecções de discriminação, incluíndo mulheres Negras trans e trabalhadoris do sexo.




Para países da UE, assegurar transposição em tempo útil e totalmente trans inclusiva e implementação de Directivas da UE no combate à violência contra mulheres e violência doméstica.

author: TGEU
title: El Trans Murder Monitoring 2026 muestra que cada 32 horas, una persona trans fue asesinada
content:
El Monitoreo de Asesinatos de Personas Trans de TGEU (TMM por sus siglas en inglés) ha registrado 273 personas trans y de diversidad de género asesinadas en todo el mundo durante el último año, en promedio, un asesinato informado cada 32 horas. Se reportaron asesinatos en 35 países, el segundo número más alto desde que comenzó el monitoreo, y por primera vez en Rumania y Camerún. En total, el TMM ha registrado ahora más de 5,500 asesinatos en todo el mundo desde que comenzó la recopilación de datos en 2009.




TGEU – Trans Europa y Asia Central publica la actualización anual de su proyecto global de Monitoreo de Asesinatos de Personas Trans en la antesala de la Semana de Conciencia Trans, que culmina con el Día de la Remembranza Trans (TDoR por sus siglas en inglés) el 20 de noviembre.




El proyecto TMM solo cuenta los asesinatos reportados, y el trabajo de monitoreo se está volviendo más difícil. El número total de asesinatos reportados está por debajo de 300 por segunda vez en una década, pero la violencia no ha disminuido. El espacio cívico se está reduciendo, hay hostilidad hacia las personas trans desde los medios y el Estado, y los recortes de financiamiento hacen menos probable que un asesinato sea reportado y registrado. 




Conclusiones clave







Se informó que 273 personas trans y de género diverso fueron asesinadas

 entre el 1 de octubre de 2025 y el 30 de septiembre de 2026

, lo que equivale a un asesinato cada 32 horas.




35 países diferentes

 reportaron un asesinato, 

el segundo número más alto hasta ahora.

 Solo en 2024 fue mayor el número de países que reportaron (38).




Una de cada tres víctimas eran trabajadoras sexuales (32%), que siguen siendo el grupo más atacado

 de todas las ocupaciones conocidas.




Siguiendo los patrones de años anteriores, 

casi todos los asesinatos reportados (95%) fueron feminicidios

 (las víctimas eran mujeres trans o personas transfemeninas), 

y tres cuartas partes (75%) de las víctimas eran personas trans negras o morenas.




El perfil de edad de las víctimas de homicidio parece estar cambiando hacia 

edades un poco mayores.

 Más de un tercio (35%) tenía entre 

31 y 40

 años en 2026, mientras que uno de cada cinco (21%) tenían entre 

19 y 25

 años, siendo consistentemente el grupo de edad más grande en la primera década de TMM. Uno de cada veinte (5%) de las víctimas del último año eran 

menores de 18 años.




Siete de cada diez (69%) asesinatos ocurrieron en América Latina y el Caribe.

 Brasil vuelve a liderar la lista, representando uno de cada tres (32%) del total mundial. Los números siguieron bajando en 

México

, con los asesinatos más bajos reportados (29) desde 2011. Sin embargo, 2026 registró el total más alto de la historia en 

Argentina

 (16) y el segundo total más alto en 

Ecuador

 (16) desde que comenzó la TMM.




El número de asesinatos reportados en 

Asia

 (32) cayó después del récord histórico del año pasado (51). Es probable que el total de este año esté subestimado: algunos socios de monitoreo en Asia informaron no tener capacidad para proporcionar datos este año, citando 

falta de recursos

 e incluso de electricidad.




Se reportaron 13 asesinatos en Europa, 

el total más alto desde 2023

, tantos como en 2024 y 2025 juntos. 

La mayoría de las víctimas eran migrantes internacionales.




Uno de cada diez casos se registró en 

Estados Unidos

 (29), un nivel similar al de 2025 (31).




Dos de cada cinco (40%) de los 

asesinatos

 reportados fueron tiroteos, mientras que una cuarta parte (24%) fueron 

apuñalamientos

. Tres de cada diez (30%) de los asesinatos ocurrieron en la calle, y una cuarta parte (25%) ocurrieron en el propio 

hogar

 de la víctima.




De los perpetradores conocidos, uno de cada cuatro (25%) era una pareja, amante o cónyuge actual o anterior. Otros perpetradores comúnmente reportados fueron grupos/ pandillas de odio organizadas (15%), desconocidos (14%), policía/militares/ejército (12%) y clientes de trabajo sexual (8%).




Se arrestó a un agresor

 en solo uno de cada cinco casos (21%) donde las autoridades locales registraron una respuesta.










Violencia interseccional




Año tras año, se asesina al mismo grupo demográfico de personas trans. Casi todas las víctimas reportadas (95%) eran mujeres trans o personas transfemeninas. Las trabajadoras sexuales, que representan a una de cada tres víctimas, siguen siendo el grupo más atacado de todas las ocupaciones conocidas, y tres de cada cuatro víctimas eran personas trans negras o mestizas.




Así es como se ve la opresión interseccional en la práctica. La misoginia, la transfobia, el racismo, la xenofobia y la horefobia se combinan entre sí, y quienes están en sus cruces son los que más en riesgo están.




‘Como mujer trans negra y refugiada, vivo con el miedo constante de perder mi vida. Mientras otros siguen con su vida diaria con una sensación de seguridad, las mujeres trans negras debemos estar siempre alertas, cuidando nuestra espalda. Nuestra seguridad nunca está garantizada. 




Estos asesinatos no son solo números en un informe; son nuestros amigos, colegas, hermanos, padres y miembros de nuestras comunidades. A medida que estos crímenes aumentan año tras año, exigimos más que simpatía: exigimos justicia, investigaciones adecuadas y responsabilidad por cada vida perdida. Las mujeres trans negras merecen el derecho a vivir seguras, libres y con dignidad.

‘




– Purity Tumukwasibwe, Miembro de la junta directiva de TGEU  







La mayoría de los asesinatos reportados: América Latina y el Caribe




Detrás del total global, la violencia no se distribuye de manera uniforme. Siete de cada diez asesinatos reportados este año ocurrieron en América Latina y el Caribe, y Brasil nuevamente representa uno de cada tres casos a nivel mundial.




Esta concentración refleja la magnitud de la violencia, y también refleja la documentación. América Latina cuenta con un movimiento de larga data de organizaciones trans y feministas que monitorean y reportan feminicidios. Como resultado, más casos llegan a los registros que en regiones donde esa infraestructura es escasa. Las cifras también son conteos brutos, no ajustados por tamaño de población, por lo que muestran dónde se reportan los asesinatos, no dónde una persona trans está en mayor riesgo.




Dentro de la región, la situación se mueve en diferentes direcciones. Algunos países parecen estar en una trayectoria descendente (por ejemplo, México), mientras que otros han alcanzado el total anual más alto desde que comenzamos a monitorear (por ejemplo, Argentina). No se debe interpretar que un número nacional más bajo signifique un país más seguro sin mirar de cerca cada contexto, como señala uno de nuestros socios de monitoreo:




‘No debemos mostrar ningún signo de celebración [por la disminución de los asesinatos registrados]; más bien, debemos examinar detenidamente las tendencias actuales, incluidas las de cada país en particular.’

 




– Rocío Suárez, Centro de Apoyo a las Identidades Trans A.C., México







Nuestra región: Europa y Asia Central




En Europa, este año se han reportado 13 asesinatos. Eso es tantos como en 2024 y 2025 juntos. La mayoría de las víctimas eran migrantes internacionales; casi todas eran mujeres trans o personas transfemeninas, y un tercio eran trabajadoras sexuales. El patrón es claro: quienes están en la intersección de múltiples formas de marginación son los que más riesgo corren. 




Muchas personas vienen a Europa buscando una vida en la que puedan ser ellas mismas y estar seguras. Para los migrantes entre estas víctimas, esa búsqueda terminó en asesinato. El patrón señala el efecto combinado de la xenofobia, el racismo y la transfobia, lo que deja a las personas trans migrantes sin protección y entre las más expuestas al daño. Esto ocurre en medio de un creciente movimiento de extrema derecha y reacción antigénero en toda Europa, que se traduce en una retórica cada vez más hostil, legislación restrictiva y ataques políticos a los derechos de migrantes y personas trans.




En Asia Central, no se nos reportaron asesinatos este año. Esto no debe interpretarse como una ausencia de violencia. Más bien refleja la falta de seguridad para las personas trans en la región, que se ven obligadas a permanecer lo más invisibles posible, mientras que sus familiares pueden no revelar su identidad trans después de la muerte. Con activistas enfrentando desafíos abrumadores y recursos limitados para el monitoreo, los asesinatos a menudo no se contabilizan. Una de las víctimas asesinadas en Europa este año fue un migrante de Asia Central, lo que refleja una historia más amplia de personas trans que dejan la región para construir una vida donde puedan vivir de manera más abierta.




‘En Asia Central, no se nos reportaron asesinatos este año. Esto no debe interpretarse como una ausencia de violencia. Más bien refleja la falta de seguridad para las personas trans en la región, que se ven obligadas a permanecer lo más invisibles posible, mientras que sus familiares pueden no revelar su identidad trans después de la muerte. Con activistas enfrentando desafíos abrumadores y recursos limitados para el monitoreo, los asesinatos a menudo no se contabilizan. Una de las víctimas asesinadas en Europa este año fue un migrante de Asia Central, lo que refleja una historia más amplia de personas trans que dejan la región para construir una vida donde puedan vivir de manera más abierta

.’




–  Tayri Fadil, miembro de la junta directiva de TGEU 







¿Quién está detrás de los asesinatos de personas trans?




Cuando se conocía al agresor, uno de cada cinco asesinatos (19%) fue cometido por una pareja, amante o cónyuge. Casi una cuarta parte de los asesinatos de este año (25%) ocurrieron en la propia casa de la víctima. Es un patrón que se repite de años anteriores: en una sociedad hostil hacia las personas trans, incluso el propio hogar no es un lugar seguro. 




Los grupos de odio organizados y las pandillas (15%) y los desconocidos (14%) también se reportaron comúnmente. En conjunto, estos patrones señalan una violencia que alcanza a las personas trans por todas partes: en sus relaciones, en sus comunidades y en la calle.




En el 12% de los casos en los que se conocía al perpetrador, la persona responsable era miembro de la policía, el ejército o la fuerza militar: 13 casos, frente a cinco del año pasado. Nueve personas trans fueron asesinadas o murieron en circunstancias sospechosas en prisiones o comisarías, comparado con cuatro el año pasado. Estas son instituciones estatales, y las muertes dentro de ellas son violencia cometida o permitida por el estado.




Estas cifras plantean preguntas difíciles sobre quién está protegido y quién no. Las personas trans están expuestas a la hostilidad, al perfilado y al abuso por parte de actores estatales, y quienes tienen el deber de hacer cumplir la ley están entre los responsables de quitar la vida a personas trans. Cuando la transfobia y la transfobia machista influyen en cómo funcionan estas instituciones, las personas trans quedan más expuestas.  




Cuando las autoridades locales respondieron, un perpetrador fue arrestado en solo uno de cada cinco casos (21%). Los procesos judiciales llevan tiempo y algunos casos avanzan lentamente por el sistema. Sin embargo, muchos asesinatos de personas trans ni siquiera se investigan; otros se investigan sin urgencia o no se registran como lo que son. El sesgo en cómo se investigan y resuelven los casos, incluyendo el rechazo de los motivos anti-trans, hace que quienes son responsables tengan menos probabilidades de rendir cuentas. Para las familias y comunidades, la ausencia de justicia puede ser otra pérdida.




‘Cada año somos testigos del resultado predecible del odio sistémico y la represión de las vidas trans. Mientras recordamos nuestras vidas, también quiero nombrar quiénes nos matan: familiares, parejas, clientes, policías y las instituciones que se los permiten. Es hora de que den cuentas por ello.

‘




-Isa Nico Borrelli, Presidente de la Junta directiva de TGEU







Tendencias demográficas




El patrón de quién está más en riesgo no ha cambiado. Una de cada tres víctimas eran trabajadoras sexuales, el grupo más atacado de todas las ocupaciones conocidas. Casi todas (95%) eran mujeres trans o personas transfemeninas, y el 76% eran personas trans negras o marrones. 




Las víctimas registradas parecen estar un poco mayores, con una de cada tres de entre 31 y 40 años, mientras que una de cada veinte era menor de edad. Además, los asesinatos reportados en Asia cayeron del récord histórico del año pasado de 51 a 32. Esto probablemente sea un conteo bajo: algunos socios de monitoreo en la región no pudieron proporcionar datos este año, citando falta de electricidad y financiamiento.







Recomendaciones




TGEU hace un llamado a los gobiernos y a las instituciones para:







Derogar leyes y políticas que criminalicen o restrinjan las identidades trans, el reconocimiento legal de género, la atención sanitaria específica para personas trans y la expresión pública de identidades trans y de género diverso.




Poner fin a la criminalización del trabajo sexual por completo y garantizar derechos laborales y protecciones para trabajadoras sexuales trans y de género diverso.




Armonizar y adoptar leyes de delitos de odio y anti-discriminación que protejan explícitamente a las personas trans en el empleo, la educación y otras áreas, y trabajar hacia un entendimiento común de lo que se considera discurso de odio ilegal.




Asegúrate de que las decisiones sobre la ubicación en prisión se basen en la autodeterminación, independientemente del estado de reconocimiento legal de género, e incluyan los deseos y el bienestar de la persona trans en cuestión.




Apoya a los defensores de los derechos humanos y a las organizaciones de la sociedad civil aliviando las presiones financieras, protegiendo su seguridad y permitiéndoles seguir organizándose y defendiendo sus derechos sin miedo.




Capacitar a los profesionales para responder adecuadamente a la violencia anti-trans, incluyendo a las fuerzas policiales, prestando especial atención a quienes enfrentan formas de discriminación interseccional, como las mujeres trans negras y las trabajadoras sexuales.




Para los países de la UE, asegúrense de una transposición e implementación totalmente trans-inclusiva y oportuna de la Directiva de la UE sobre la lucha contra la violencia hacia las mujeres y la violencia doméstica.

TMM usa feminicidio en lugar de femicidio ya que refleja mejor las causas estructurales y políticas de la violencia contra mujeres y niñas. El término, acuñado por Marcela Lagarde en América Latina, destaca la responsabilidad del Estado y los fallos sistémicos de prevención, protección y rendición de cuentas que permiten estos asesinatos.

title: TGEU publishes Legal developments on trans-specific healthcare: A review of national case law in the EU
content:
Court cases have been central to advancing the rights of trans people in Europe, but trans-specific healthcare remains largely untested in the courts.




Since the European Court of Human Rights’ earliest decisions on legal gender recognition, strategic litigation has driven many major advances. More recently, rulings by the Court of Justice of the European Union on freedom of movement and non-discrimination have further strengthened these gains. TGEU’s 

2026 Trans Rights Map

 also found that national court decisions are increasingly driving progress in trans rights, particularly where legislative and policy advances are stalled or reversed.




Trans-specific healthcare is an exception and is comparatively less litigated at the European level. Trans people across the EU face significant barriers in accessing trans-specific healthcare. Enforcing their rights to healthcare is further complicated by administrative refusals, unclear national regulations, and national court rulings that remain largely unknown. At the same time, interest is growing in using legal tools to advocate for improved access to trans-specific healthcare, and in how courts across the region handle such cases.










get the publication










Objective of the publication




This resource explains how litigation can help improve access to trans-specific healthcare by reviewing case law from national

author: TGEU
title: Joint statement: We call on Türkiye to end the targeting of trans people and sex workers
content:
Trans women and trans sex workers are being arrested, prosecuted and held in degrading conditions in Türkiye. Since 12 September, the ‘My Family Is Safe’ operation has escalated into a sweeping crackdown on LGBTI communities and civil society, through raids, arrests and prolonged detention. As governments and international institutions turn their attention to Türkiye in the lead-up to COP31, we call on them to act: to press for the release of everyone arbitrarily detained, ensure accountability, and support the communities affected.




ESWA (European Sex Workers’ Rights Alliance)

, 

NSWP (Global Network of Sex Work Projects)

, 

SWAN (Sex Workers’ Rights Advocacy Network)

 and TGEU – Trans Europe and Central Asia strongly condemn the escalating crackdown on LGBTI human rights defenders and communities in Türkiye, including the raids, arrests and ongoing detention of activists and community members. 




We are particularly alarmed by the targeted prosecution of trans women and trans sex workers, and reports of serious mistreatment and degrading conditions in custody. Together with the attention to the attacks against civil society organisations and their representatives, there is an urgent need for attention to the targeting of trans women and sex workers, whose experiences risk being overlooked in the international response. 




We stand in solidarity with our community members and urgently call on the international community to maintain pressure to end the attacks and ensure that these human rights violations remain subject to international scrutiny and concrete action.




What is happening in Türkiye




Since September 12, the operation “

My Family Is Safe

” has instigated an escalating wave of attacks on civil society, targeting LGBTI organisations, human rights defenders, and journalists through coordinated raids, detentions, and arrests. In the latest wave of attacks on October 23, 45 people, including 12 trans women, were taken into custody. On 26 October, 19 people, including 

10 trans women

, were arrested in relation to allegations of prostitution. 

The Ankara Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office

 cited social media posts by people taken into custody as grounds for the arrests, claiming that the posts contained material that was “contrary to public morality, targeting families, (. . .) encouraging gender neutrality and disruptive to public order,” creating the perception that people could choose their gender. In other words, 

the identities and forms of expression of trans people were presented as grounds for their arrest and prosecution.

 Further, on 3 November, 22 more people, including trans women, were detained on allegations of “encouraging, facilitating or coercing prostitution” and “forming an organisation for the purpose of committing a crime”.




Reports of the treatment of trans women detained during the operation raise serious concerns about conditions and human rights violations in state custody. According to lawyers working with Ankara-based LGBTI+ rights organisation 

ÜniKuir

, some trans women were not allowed access to toilets on their first day in custody and were forced to relieve themselves in food containers. People arrested during the raids also reported poor and overcrowded holding-cell conditions and inadequate food rations. These conditions are compounded by reported barriers to accessing sanitary facilities, timely legal support and necessary medical care, particularly affecting trans women. Such treatment threatens the health, safety and dignity of people deprived of their liberty and raises serious concerns regarding Türkiye’s obligations under international human rights law and standards, including 

the UN Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners (Nelson Mandela Rules)

.




A long-standing history of discrimination against trans people




While the scope and aggression of this operation are unprecedented, the systemic targeting of trans people in Türkiye is not new.  For years, Türkiye has undermined the rights of trans people in administrative actions restricting access to hormones and arrests of trans activists, alongside systemic discrimination in access to education, healthcare, housing, and employment. 




The arrests since September 12 intensify this structural discrimination, exposing how authorities invoke “promotion of prostitution” and obscenity-related charges to track, prosecute and imprison trans women and sex workers. Combined with the prolonged detention of trans women and LGBTI activists, the use of these misdemeanour charges raises serious concerns that authorities are using and stretching different legal grounds to target trans women based solely on their identities. 




The raids are systematically destabilising LGBTI civil society in Türkiye, restricting their ability to organise. As their staff, activists and volunteers are directly targeted, those who continue the vital work of providing aid, legal assistance, and monitoring the treatment of people in custody face severe safety risks. The Turkish authorities have also blocked the social media accounts of most LGBTI and human rights organisations, which further isolates affected communities and obstructs access to information and support when this is most urgently needed.




Our demands




Building on previous calls from Turkish and international civil society organisations, we urge sustained political attention to the attacks on LGBTI rights in Türkiye and call for practical action. We reaffirm the demands set out in previous statements and urgent appeals by Turkish and international civil society organisations. 




We call on:




The United Nations Special Procedures, 

particularly the Special Rapporteur on the situation of human rights defenders (SR HRDs), the Independent Expert on protection against violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity (IE SOGI), and the Special Rapporteur on the right to health





Send an urgent communication to the Turkish authorities concerning the arrests, prolonged detention and reported mistreatment of trans women, sex workers and LGBTI human rights defenders.




Seek clarification on the legal grounds for the arrests and detention, and demand information on measures taken to prevent further violations and investigate reported abuses.




Publicly call for the immediate release of anyone arbitrarily detained, an end to discriminatory arrests and prosecutions, and effective safeguards against further arbitrary detention and ill-treatment.










The Council of Europe:

 including the Commissioner for Human Rights (CommHR) and the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture (CPT)





Raise the crackdown and report abuses directly with the Turkish authorities and engage with affected organisations.




Use relevant monitoring and country-engagement mechanisms to scrutinise detention conditions, including access to sanitation, food, medical care and legal assistance.




Press for the implementation of CPT standards on non-discrimination, protection from ill-treatment, including the guidance note on transgender prisoners, and the rights of human rights defenders, with particular attention to access to sanitation, food, and medical care.










The European Parliament, the European Commission and the European External Action Service (EEAS)







Maintain political and diplomatic pressure, including through follow-up to the 

European Parliament’s September debate




Ensure that trans women, sex workers and their organisations are explicitly included in consultations and protection efforts.




Strengthen emergency support for affected communities and organisations.










Diplomatic missions in Türkiye







Maintain regular contact with affected LGBTI and sex worker-led organisations and provide emergency financial support to keep organisations working.




Attend court hearings, raise individual cases with the local authorities and coordinate diplomatic interventions where human rights defenders or community members face immediate risks.




Support emergency protection measures, including safe relocation where necessary, and facilitating access to relevant international protection mechanisms.










Donors and foundations







Provide rapid, flexible funding for legal defence, emergency assistance, medical and psychosocial support.




Sustain core funding so affected organisations can continue their work, including documenting abuses, supporting people arrested and providing services to communities affected by police operations.




Prioritise direct funding for trans-led and sex worker-led organisations, ensuring that funding arrangements do not expose these groups or their members to additional risks.










International civil society networks







Coordinate solidarity actions, joint advocacy and submissions to international human rights mechanisms.




Support local organisations to document violations and bring affected communities’ evidence and demands to international attention.




Amplify the priorities of affected communities and ensure that trans women and sex workers remain visible in international advocacy and monitoring.













Your support makes change possible




We work across Europe and Central Asia to advance trans rights, build strong communities, and drive change through research, advocacy, and community-building.




Your donation helps us continue this vital work — defending trans lives, amplifying trans voices, and advocating for justice every day.

title: Trans activists and stakeholders gather at TGEU’s Pre-Council to advance trans rights in Eastern Europe and Central Asia
content:
On 9-10 September in Ljubljana, Slovenia, 27 trans activists from Eastern Europe and Central Asia (EECA) and international stakeholders came together to ask one question: how do we protect trans people in a region where democracy and human rights are deteriorating?




The second TGEU Pre-Council Strategic Meeting on Trans Rights in EECA took place ahead of TGEU’s 10th European and Central Asian Trans Council. Over two days, participants analysed the rapidly changing political and legal environment, exchanged lessons learned, and explored ways to strengthen cooperation, joint advocacy and coordinated action.

 




The Strategic Meeting brought together three groups with different but complementary types of expertise and mandates: 







EECA trans activists with direct experience working with communities and conducting national advocacy




International stakeholders working on human rights and the rule of law




Allied movement leaders engaged in human rights protection.







Together, they aimed to build a shared understanding of key challenges and possible responses, identify political and legal leverage points for 2026–2027, and strengthen trust and cooperation.



















Key takeaways







Participants shared strategies for responding to anti-trans policies.

author: TGEU
title: Join the HIV Awareness Week in Berlin to establish the Emergency Support Network
content:
We are organising two free-of-charge parallel training programmes for queer and trans people that will come together on Friday, 20 November, to establish the Emergency Support Network.




This network should help people navigate services, identify realistic pathways to HIV prevention and care, and receive support without having to navigate complex systems alone. We also want to recognise that Ballroom houses, queer and trans collectives, and migrant communities already provide essential care infrastructure. We intend to strengthen these existing relationships, rather than create a parallel system disconnected from the communities themselves.




The initiative is particularly focused on two target audience groups:







Queer and trans people living with HIV who face barriers to accessing healthcare, especially those without health insurance, appropriate documentation, or access to HIV treatment and other essential services.




Queer and trans people on the move, including migrants, refugees, asylum seekers and undocumented people, who face difficulties accessing healthcare, HIV prevention, testing, PrEP, PEP and treatment.







Community HIV Training — 16, 18 and 20 November




This programme is intended for queer and trans adults, particularly queer and trans youth aged 18 and over, migrants, refugees, asylum seekers, undocumented people and other people on the move.




It is especially relevant to queer and trans people who are living with HIV and face difficulties accessing treatment or healthcare, as well as those who need access to HIV prevention, testing, PrEP, PEP and other sexual health services.




The sessions will be interactive and community-led, covering HIV prevention and care, PrEP, PEP, testing, treatment, U=U, sexual health, pleasure, harm reduction and navigating healthcare systems.




An important feature is that registration for this programme is anonymous.

 Participants are not asked to provide their names, email addresses or HIV status. Anyone who wants to receive practical information or reminders can voluntarily register their email address through a separate form, which is not linked to their anonymous demographic responses.




This distinction is particularly important for people who may be reluctant to engage with services or activities because of concerns about confidentiality, stigma or their migration status.










register here










Health Champions Training — 17, 19 and 20 November




This programme is designed for trans and queer community leaders, particularly people involved in Ballroom houses, collectives and grassroots networks.




The training follows a train-the-trainer approach and will cover HIV, STIs and other infectious diseases prevention, treatment and sexual and reproductive health knowledge, and other topics like U=U, harm reduction, structural barriers to healthcare, peer education and safe healthcare navigation.




Participants will work through practical exercises such as community mapping, HIV knowledge games, real-life scenarios, role-play and referral mapping. The objective is to equip them to become trusted points of connection between their communities and healthcare services, while recognising that Health Champions are not expected to act as clinicians, legal experts or crisis responders.




On the final day, Health Champions will meet healthcare professionals, service providers and participants from the other training programme to help establish practical referral pathways and community-based support structures.










register here










Building the Emergency Support Network 

—

 

20 November 




On Friday, participants from both programmes will come together with healthcare professionals, community organisations and service providers.




The aim is to establish direct connections between people who need support, trusted community leaders and organisations capable of providing services. Participants will learn what support is available, who can access it, what barriers remain and how to make safe referrals.




The week will culminate in 

Under the Jellicle Moon Kiki Ball on Saturday, 21 November

, celebrating Ballroom culture, community leadership and the relationships developed throughout the initiative.




Note: 

All workshop participants must be 18 or older and attend all three days of their respective training. Snacks and dinner will be provided each day.




Your support makes change possible




We work across Europe and Central Asia to advance trans rights, build strong communities, and drive change through research, advocacy, and community-building.




Your donation helps us continue this vital work — defending trans lives, amplifying trans voices, and advocating for justice every day.

author: TGEU
title: Hungary removes anti-LGBTI provisions, but trans people are still left out
content:
TGEU welcomes the decision of the Hungarian National Assembly on 13 October, 2026 to remove the anti-LGBTI content from the 2021 ‘child protection’ law. This is a necessary step to implement the Court of Justice of the EU (CJEU) judgment in 

Commission v Hungary

 (C-769/22).




In its April 2026 judgment, the CJEU found that the law, which stigmatised LGBTI people under the guise of child protection, breached EU law. It also rejected Hungary’s reliance on national identity to justify discriminatory measures. 




Why this matters for trans people




The ruling matters for trans people across the EU, because it confirms that Member States cannot use ‘child protection’ or national identity as an excuse for excluding trans and other LGBTI people from public life and the rights EU law guarantees them. The CJEU has already held in 

Mirin

 (C-4/23) that Member States must recognise a legal gender change obtained in another Member State, so the Commission has clear legal grounds to act. The CJEU has also held in 

Deldits

 (C-247/23) that a Hungarian refusal to rectify a trans refugee’s gender marker breaches the GDPR, which further strengthens the case for Commission action.




The reality of LGBTI rights in Hungary

author: Aoife Doran
title: Ceuta: Spain must protect trans asylum seekers, not return them to danger
content:
More than two months after tens of thousands of people crossed from Morocco into Ceuta, many remain in precarious conditions, with inadequate access to shelter, essential services and international protection. Among them are trans asylum applicants who have fled persecution, only to face further violence, insecurity and the threat of being returned to danger. Their situation is part of a wider humanitarian crisis affecting people on the move in Ceuta, all of whom deserve safety, dignity and access to protection.




We are deeply concerned by reports of physical assaults, harassment and mistreatment of people seeking protection in Ceuta. A 

report by Border Resistance

, a grassroots collective working at the border, documents at least seven alleged incidents of violence against LGBTI people between 21 August and 6 September. One trans woman described being assaulted by police officers after being expelled from a reception centre, stating, 

“We are trans, we cannot live on the street because we are attacked.”

 Another described fleeing Morocco after receiving death threats from her family. These testimonies expose the grave risks facing trans and other LGBTI people who seek protection in Ceuta, only to encounter further violence and insecurity. We also reject the racist and dehumanising portrayal of people arriving in Ceuta as an 

‘invasion’

author: TGEU
title: TGEU publishes Know Your Rights: How EU Directives Protect Trans People. Second Revised Version
content:
This guide provides a basic overview of EU directives in which trans people are protected from discrimination, including through the explicit inclusion of the grounds of ‘gender reassignment’, ‘gender identity’, or ‘gender expression’. As such, it helps trans people to better understand and claim their fundamental rights. It also helps legal professionals, equality bodies, and policymakers to understand their legal obligations to ensure equal protection. 










Get the guide










What are EU directives?




EU directives are a type of EU law that sets goals Member States must reach through their own legislation. However, EU directives do not prescribe how Member States should implement them. In other words, EU directives set a common minimum standard but leave Member States flexibility in how they achieve it.




All EU directives must be ‘transposed’, a process that incorporates an EU directive into national legislation. Once a directive is adopted, transposition begins, and the directive itself sets a deadline for completion.







Objective of the guide




Since TGEU published our first Know Your Rights guide in 2015, additional EU directives have been adopted and are entering into force. These newer directives, which extend protections for trans people across a broader range of areas, form the focus of this guide.
